headline: PM Tarique Rahman heading to New York for UNGA 81st session on Monday
summary: The Prime Minister will deliver a speech at the UN General Assembly on September 24, during a shortened visit to the United States.
details: Prime Minister Tarique Rahman is traveling to New York on Monday, September 21, to attend the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA). He is scheduled to deliver his address to the assembly on September 24.
According to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the visit has been shortened. The Prime Minister will depart New York for Dhaka on the night of September 25, shortly after his speech.

The trip was originally planned to be longer, with preparations being made for a visit to San Francisco. However, the delegation size has also been reduced to reflect a more austere approach compared to previous governments.
During his stay, the Prime Minister will participate in high-level UN meetings on development, pandemic prevention, sea-level rise, and nuclear disarmament.
Bangladesh is also organizing several discussions in the margins of the session, including talks on the Rohingya crisis.
The Prime Minister is expected to hold bilateral meetings with several world leaders, including the Prime Ministers of Pakistan, Canada, Thailand, Bhutan, and Croatia, and the Crown Prince of Kuwait.
Additionally, he will meet with UN Secretary-General António Guterres, the World Bank President Ajay Banga, and other high-ranking officials from the UN and the European Council.
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman will also attend a dinner hosted by US President Donald Trump.
caption:
PM Tarique Rahman travels to New York this Monday for the 81st UN General Assembly. He will meet with world leaders and address the assembly on Sept 24.

Prime Minister Tarique Rahman is traveling to New York on Monday, September 21, to attend the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA). He is scheduled to deliver his address to the assembly on September 24.

According to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the visit has been shortened. The Prime Minister will depart New York for Dhaka on the night of September 25, shortly after his speech.

The trip was originally planned to be longer, with preparations being made for a visit to San Francisco. However, the delegation size has also been reduced to reflect a more austere approach compared to previous governments.

During his stay, the Prime Minister will participate in high-level UN meetings on development, pandemic prevention, sea-level rise, and nuclear disarmament.

Bangladesh is also organizing several discussions in the margins of the session, including talks on the Rohingya crisis.

The Prime Minister is expected to hold bilateral meetings with several world leaders, including the Prime Ministers of Pakistan, Canada, Thailand, Bhutan, and Croatia, and the Crown Prince of Kuwait.

Additionally, he will meet with UN Secretary-General António Guterres, the World Bank President Ajay Banga, and other high-ranking officials from the UN and the European Council.

Prime Minister Tarique Rahman will also attend a dinner hosted by US President Donald Trump.

headline_marked: Australia [[tightens immigration policies]], sparking anxiety for Bangladeshi students
headline: Australia tightens immigration policies, sparking anxiety for Bangladeshi students
summary: New restrictions on 'visa hopping' and family sponsorship aim to reduce net migration to 245,000 by 2026-27.
details: Australia's central government has introduced significant restrictions on immigration policies to combat a housing crisis and rising living costs. Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke outlined the new measures at the National Press Club in Canberra.
The government aims to reduce the annual net migration to 245,000 by the 2026-27 fiscal year, with a further decrease to 225,000 in subsequent years.
Key changes include a crackdown on 'visa hopping'—where students switch to lower-quality courses to extend their stay—and stricter limits on bringing family members to Australia.
New 'no further stay' conditions will be added to all tourist visas, effectively preventing visitors from applying for other visas while remaining in the country.

The policy also introduces a lottery system for second and third-year Working Holiday visas in agriculture and service sectors, though skilled migrants in healthcare and construction will be prioritized.
Immigration officials now have special powers to quickly cancel visas and deport migrants involved in domestic violence, child abuse, or hate crimes.
Thousands of international students have protested in major cities like Sydney, Melbourne, and Brisbane, skipping classes to voice their anger over the government's decision.
Bangladeshi students in Sydney and Lakemba have expressed deep uncertainty, fearing that frequent rule changes and limited visa options could force them to return home.
caption:
Australia is slashing its migration targets and banning 'visa hopping.' Bangladeshi students now face a future of extreme uncertainty.

Australia's central government has introduced significant restrictions on immigration policies to combat a housing crisis and rising living costs. Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke outlined the new measures at the National Press Club in Canberra.

The government aims to reduce the annual net migration to 245,000 by the 2026-27 fiscal year, with a further decrease to 225,000 in subsequent years.

Key changes include a crackdown on 'visa hopping'—where students switch to lower-quality courses to extend their stay—and stricter limits on bringing family members to Australia.

New 'no further stay' conditions will be added to all tourist visas, effectively preventing visitors from applying for other visas while remaining in the country.

The policy also introduces a lottery system for second and third-year Working Holiday visas in agriculture and service sectors, though skilled migrants in healthcare and construction will be prioritized.

Immigration officials now have special powers to quickly cancel visas and deport migrants involved in domestic violence, child abuse, or hate crimes.

Thousands of international students have protested in major cities like Sydney, Melbourne, and Brisbane, skipping classes to voice their anger over the government's decision.

Bangladeshi students in Sydney and Lakemba have expressed deep uncertainty, fearing that frequent rule changes and limited visa options could force them to return home.
